note: raw Kokoro clip lengths per VO line (untrimmed). Fit raw = a + words*60/wpm + pause*(sentences-1). Speeds 0.96/1.15 were measured on an earlier draft (1,342 words); 1.2/1.25 on the final draft. Lines c3, c8, g9, h4, h9, f4, a6, x7 re-measured after their final edit.

c1.tts: You fall off a ferry in the Pacific and gasp in seawater.

c3.tts: No coughing. No burning. Your chest just keeps going, like you've done this forever.

c4.tts: Something bumps your back and holds on. A remora. It thinks you're a shark.

c5.tts: Everyone up there breathes air. Everyone but you.

c6.tts: And here's the catch: air doesn't work for you anymore. You can't climb back on.

c7.tts: Under you, the floor is four kilometres down. The deepest floor on Earth is a trench, a few hundred kilometres south-west of you.

c8.tts: And a line on your way down is a wall.

t0.tts: What if you could breathe underwater?

r1.tts: One change: your body can pull oxygen out of water.

r2.tts: One promise: every time the ocean tries to kill you, you get the fix a real animal already uses.

r4.tts: Everything else stays human: daylight eyes, and blood at thirty-seven degrees.

r5.tts: Keep an eye on that number. It's already moving.

g1.tts: First, the bad news: seawater holds about thirty times less oxygen than air.

g2.tts: So about sixty litres of sea has to pour through you every minute.

g3.tts: A bathtub every two and a half minutes.

g4.tts: Lungs can't. Water is heavy, and lungs push it in and out the same pipe.

g5.tts: In nineteen sixty-six, a lab mouse breathed oxygen-rich liquid and lived. Breathing out was the hard part.

g6.tts: You try to shout for help. Nothing comes out. No air, no voice.

g8.tts: So here's your first fix, borrowed from every fish alive: gills.

g9.tts: Water goes in your mouth and out behind your jaw, with your blood flowing against it.

g10.tts: That grabs up to eighty percent of the oxygen. Your lungs managed a quarter.

g11.tts: Easy. Except breathing water does one more thing to you, and you won't feel it yet.

h1.tts: two hundred metres. For a while, this is the best swim of your life.

h2.tts: Every ten metres adds an atmosphere of pressure, crushing the air inside divers.

h3.tts: But you have no air left to crush. Water floods your sinuses and ears, and water barely squeezes.

h4.tts: The deepest anyone has dived on a single breath is two hundred and fifty-three metres. You pass it without noticing.

h5.tts: Then a blue whale slides under you, longer than two buses.

h6.tts: It doesn't even look at you. Good.

h7.tts: Problem one: salt. The sea you keep swallowing is about three times saltier than your blood.

h8.tts: Fish have the fix: gill cells that pump salt back out. Now so do you.

h9.tts: Problem two: light. About one percent of the sunlight gets this deep, and your eyes were made for beaches. No fix for that.

h11.tts: Your fingertips have gone white. You decide it's just the light.

m1.tts: one thousand metres. The light isn't dim anymore. It's gone.

m2.tts: Then the dark starts to sparkle: around three in four animals here make their own light.

m3.tts: Problem three: something glowing drifts up to your face. An anglerfish, small enough for your palm.

m5.tts: But here's the thing. None of that was ever the real problem.

m6.tts: The real problem has been killing you since the ferry, and it's on screen right now.

m7.tts: Your blood. thirty-seven degrees, remember? The water here is four.

m8.tts: Gills swap heat too. Your blood leaves them as cold as the sea.

m9.tts: At the surface, you were losing heat about thirty times faster than you make it.

m10.tts: Here, it's a hundred. Your gills are a radiator, and the ocean is the room.

m11.tts: Hypothermia starts at thirty-five degrees. You passed it a while ago.

f1.tts: Except a few fish cheat the cold, and their cheat is real.

f2.tts: In a bluefin tuna, warm blood heading out hands its heat to cold blood coming in, through a tangle of tiny vessels.

f3.tts: It's your gill trick run backwards, saving heat instead of grabbing oxygen.

f4.tts: So your third fix: a tuna's heat exchanger, between your gills and the rest of you.

f5.tts: The readout stops falling. But tuna stay warm by never stopping, and now neither can you.

n1.tts: two thousand metres. A click hits you so hard you feel it in your teeth.

n2.tts: Then faster and faster, until the clicks blur into a buzz.

n3.tts: That's a sperm whale. When its clicks become a buzz, it's closing in on something.

n4.tts: You're warm, you're moving, and you're about the size of what it eats.

n6.tts: The buzz hits you in the chest. Then the whale turns away.

n7.tts: It wanted a giant squid, with eyes as wide as dinner plates. You don't make the cut.

n8.tts: Here's the problem nobody warned you about: every fix makes you better at the deep, and worse at everything else.

n9.tts: Many deep fish brought up to the surface don't survive the trip. You're turning into one.

a1.tts: four thousand metres. You land on the floor of the Pacific: mud, cold, and four hundred atmospheres.

a2.tts: Your gills are fine. Your molecules are not.

a3.tts: Pressure this strong squeezes your proteins out of shape. Your hands shake. Your thoughts slow.

a4.tts: In nineteen ninety-two, a diver in a French chamber survived the pressure of seven hundred and one metres, a human record.

a5.tts: You're almost six times deeper. But deep fish carry a molecule called T-M-A-O that props proteins back into shape.

a6.tts: Your fourth fix: you pack your cells with it. The shaking stops.

a7.tts: But there's a ceiling: the deeper you go, the more you need, and around eight thousand two hundred metres your cells get as concentrated as the sea.

a8.tts: In twenty fourteen, scientists predicted that's where fish run out. It's the wall on your route.

w1.tts: The trench is still days away. So you walk.

w2.tts: Then a brand-new problem: you're starving.

w3.tts: Staying warm burns food, and about one percent of what grows in sunlight ever reaches this mud.

w5.tts: So, honestly, where could you live?

w6.tts: The open ocean? Nothing to eat. The abyss? You're in it.

w7.tts: Unless you find a vent, a hot spring on the seafloor crowded with life.

w8.tts: But your best home is a coral reef, thirty metres down, still in the sunshine.

w9.tts: Except you can't go back up. Not in a body tuned for the abyss.

w10.tts: And then, ahead of you, the floor just ends.

x1.tts: eight thousand two hundred metres. The trench walls close in.

x2.tts: Right at the line, a pale fish drifts past like a wet tissue. A snailfish.

x3.tts: One trench north, in twenty twenty-two, a camera filmed its cousin at eight thousand three hundred and thirty-six metres. No fish has ever been seen deeper.

x4.tts: This is the wall. There's no animal left to borrow from.

x5.tts: The remora lets go and drifts back up toward the light.

x6.tts: From here on, this is our guess, not known science.

x7.tts: You can stay at the line, where your body still makes sense. Or pay for the last two thousand seven hundred metres with the only thing you have left: the way back.

x8.tts: You keep packing your cells past the limit. They swell with sea. They hold.

x9.tts: And they'll never work in the shallows again.

x11.tts: ten thousand nine hundred and thirty-five metres. Challenger Deep.

x12.tts: No light. No sound. Just a puff of grey mud where you land.

x13.tts: Over one thousand atmospheres: a small car parked on each of your thumbnails.

x14.tts: And finally, food. Amphipods, little shrimp-like scavengers, swarm over anything that sinks.

x15.tts: Down here, you're the thing that sank.

x16.tts: You eat them. They nibble you back. Fair.

x17.tts: In twenty nineteen, scientists opened up amphipods from this trench. Every single one had man-made fibres in its gut.

x18.tts: Your first meal in six days, and your world got to it first.

b1.tts: You look up. eleven kilometres above you, the ferry is still crossing. The remora is up there somewhere.

b2.tts: So, could you breathe underwater? Yes. That part's easy.

b3.tts: You'd need gills, salt pumps, a tuna's heat exchanger and a deep fish's chemistry. And you'd pay with the way home.

b4.tts: Getting in was never the hard part. Getting out is.

e1.tts: So, back at that ferry rail: would you jump? And where would you stop: the reef, the vent, or the line?

e2.tts: Want to see what happens when you try to swim back up? Tell me.
